title: Cramming for Exams Experts Share Better Ways to Learn
paragraphs: Many students have stayed up late the night before a big exam, trying to learn as much as possible in a short time. This is known as cramming. But according to learning experts, cramming is not a very effective way to study, and there are much better methods.

One of the most important studies on this topic was published in 2013 by psychologist John Dunlosky and colleagues. They reviewed ten popular study techniques and found that only two deserved a "high utility" rating: practice testing and distributed practice. Popular methods such as rereading notes and highlighting text did not perform as well.

Distributed practice, also known as spaced practice, means spreading study sessions out over a longer period of time, rather than studying everything at once. For example, instead of studying for five hours the night before an exam, a student might study for one hour a day over five days. Research suggests that this helps people remember information for much longer.

Why does cramming feel so effective, then? One reason is that when people review the same material many times in a short period, it starts to feel familiar. However, experts say the brain can mistake this feeling of familiarity for real learning. In one vocabulary study at the University of California, Los Angeles, spacing out study sessions was more effective for 90% of participants.

The second recommended technique, practice testing, is also known as retrieval practice. Instead of simply reading information again, students test themselves by trying to recall it from memory, for example by using flashcards or answering practice questions. According to some educators, more than 200 studies have shown that this method leads to better long-term memory than rereading.

Experts suggest combining both methods. This means testing yourself regularly and gradually increasing the time between review sessions. Starting early is also important, so that there is enough time to space out study sessions before the exam.

However, these techniques have their limits. Experts note that spaced repetition works best for learning facts, vocabulary and formulas. It does not replace the need to truly understand a subject and practice applying what you have learned.
